10.1002_adfm.202529623: Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 2 F 3 (NVPF) is a considered cathode material for sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) due to its high operating voltage and substantial capacity. However, its deployment is hindered by low conductivity and poor interfacial stability at high voltage. Herein, we report a rational structural modulation strategy by introducing high‐valence Mo dopants into the NVPF lattice. The substitution of V with Mo not only induces local electric field reconstruction but also plays a pivotal catalytic role in promoting controlled electrolyte decomposition. This catalysis accelerates the formation of a uniform and robust cathode‐electrolyte interphase (CEI). Consequently, the Mo‐NVPF@rGO delivers an enhanced rate capability (85.7 mAh g −1 at 10 C), long‐term cycling stability (87% capacity retention after 500 cycles at 5 C), and reliable performance over a wide temperature range. Coupled with commercial hard carbon, the Mo‐NVPF@rGO||CHC full battery delivered 121.8 mAh g −1 at 0.2 C with a high energy density of 468 Wh kg −1 . DFT calculations further reveal that Mo doping catalyzes the decomposition of electrolyte, promoting the formation of a fluorine‐rich CEI. This work highlights the dual function of aliovalent doping in tuning bulk electronic/ionic properties and enabling interfacial engineering via catalytic CEI formation, offering a generalizable, scalable strategy for high‐performance electrodes for SIBs.
10.1002_adfm.75830: Sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) have demonstrated great potential for energy storage applications due to their unique performance characteristics and the abundant natural reserves of Na in the earth's crust. Hard carbon (HC) is regarded as the most promising anode material for SIBs owing to its high Na storage capacity. However, the highly complex and heterogeneous microstructure of HC poses a significant challenge for performance enhancement. Precise regulation of the HC microstructure at the molecular level is thus crucial for enhancing its performance. Based on the intrinsic structure–performance relationship of HC, this review summarizes recent research progress in molecular engineering strategies for the development of HC. It outlines the principles of controllable design for different precursors at the molecular scale, analyzes in detail the influence of pyrolysis process parameters on the structural evolution of carbon layers. With a focus on crystallites, pores, defects, and interfacial chemistry of HC, various modification approaches are discussed, including molecular coupling, molecular templating, heteroatom doping, metal‐ion catalysis, functional group regulation, and molecular coating modification. This review provides a comprehensive framework for the precise regulation and performance optimization of HC, aiming to offer theoretical guidance for the development of high‐performance HC and to facilitate the commercialization of SIBs.
10.1002_advs.76600: Alloying 2D transition metal dichalcogenides offers a promising strategy to broaden their applications. Herein, (RuMoVNb)Se 2 quaternary alloy nanosheets ( x Ru = 0–1) were synthesized via colloidal reactions. Incorporation of Ru into the (MoVNb)Se 2 maintained exclusively 2D layered structure over wide composition range, accompanied by a phase evolution from the hexagonal 2H to 1T. The quaternary alloying results in more metallic electronic structures than the ternary alloying. First‐principles calculations supported the homogenous atomic mixing of quaternary alloys and the favored 2H → 1T phase transition at higher x Ru . Compared to (MoVNb)Se 2 , the quaternary alloys exhibited significantly enhanced electrocatalytic activity toward the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) across alkaline, acidic, and neutral electrolytes. Gibbs free energy calculations show that Ru atoms optimize hydrogen adsorption, directly correlating with the improved HER performance. In situ X‐ray absorption fine structure data (in 1 M KOH) reveal electrolyte adsorption on Ru as key to superior HER catalysis.
10.1002_smll.76534: Lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs) require stable high‐voltage cathode materials to meet escalating energy storage demands. LiNi 0.5 Mn 1.5 O 4 (LNMO) offers high energy density while employing earth‐abundant manganese but suffers from degradation due to manganese dissolution and electrolyte decomposition at elevated voltages. This work presents a facile water‐based process to coat LNMO particles with nanometer‐thin niobate nanosheets via electrostatically driven self‐assembly. As nanosheets of large aspect ratio (≈2000) are obtained by a spontaneous delamination yielding uniform thickness (1.8 nm), the coating consistently covers LNMO surfaces. Electrochemical testing in full‐cells showed improved cycle stability, enhanced rate capability, and reduced self‐discharge for coated LNMO compared to pristine material. Post‐cycling analyses revealed suppressed manganese migration to the anode, evidencing the coating's effectiveness as a Li‐ion‐conductive, chemically inert permselective membrane that mitigates detrimental side reactions. The modified LNMO/graphite full cells exhibit excellent cycling stability, retaining 91% of its initial capacity after 500 cycles at 1C, as compared to 42% for the pristine material. Additionally, the coated material shows an increased rate capability, with a capacity of 101 mAh g −1 at 5C as compared to 84 mAh g −1 of the uncoated. This scalable, cost‐effective, coating strategy extends cathode lifespan and offers a promising route for advancing high‐voltage LIB technology.
10.1016_j.est.2026.123235: A persistent challenge in lithium-ion batteries is the loss of active lithium due to the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation and associated side reactions. While prelithiation employing lithium replenishment separator (LRS) has been proven effective in compensating for lithium loss, previous studies have largely been accompanied by gas evolution or solid residue formation during the prelithiation process. To surmount this challenge, we present a LRS based on 4-fluoro-1,2-dihydroxybenzene lithium salt (LiDF), capable of mitigating lithium loss while producing decomposition products that integrate directly into the electrolyte as functional additives which can assist with the stability of the SEI, free from gas or solid formation, thus establishing a sustainable and environmentally benign strategy for lithium compensation. Incorporation of the LRS enables the pristine LiFePO 4 ||graphite (Gr) full cell to achieve 10.8% higher capacity than the cell with a polypropylene separator (PPS) after 200 cycles at 0.5C. Remarkably, the degraded LiFePO 4 (D-LFP)||Gr full cell with the LRS exhibits a 135.8% capacity improvement over the PPS-based cell after 500 cycles. These findings establish the LRS as a powerful approach for both boosting high-performance lithium-ion batteries and recovering the capacity of degraded batteries.
